steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on forming student teams and assigning them to projects while accounting for preferences and conflicts. Motivate it with large project-based classes, state the problem, explain our approximation framework and contributions, and mention uses beyond education.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation: team formation in large project-based classes
2. Problem definition: preference graph, conflict graph, TFC
3. Algorithmic framework: concave relaxation + dependent rounding
4. Relation to Max-k-Cut with given part sizes; contributions
5. Experiments, generality beyond education, speedups
6. Discussion: why maximize conflicts across teams

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Motivation
- large project-based classes: instructors create teams, assign to finite number of projects
- students happy: team with friends, project they like
- teams efficient: no time conflicts (from class schedules)
- traditionally ad hoc / manual by admin, can take several days

2. Problem
- formal combinatorial optimization problem; two inputs
- preference graph: users -> projects, bipartite, edge weights proportional to how much student likes project
- conflict graph: (weighted) edge between incompatible students
- assignment: every student to one project, no project over capacity
- objective: max sum of preference-edge weights in assignment + sum of conflict-edge weights across teams
- same project = team -> Team Formation amidst Conflicts (TFC); NP-hard

3. Framework
- replace objective by concave objective, optimized in polynomial time -> fractional solution
- round with dependent-rounding techniques
- requirement: original objective and concave relaxation match on integral inputs

4. Max-k-Cut link / contributions
- framework not new; inspired by Max-k-Cut with given part sizes
- our problem identical except additional linear term
- their approximation algorithm applies to our problem
- ours: much more efficient randomized algorithm, better approximation ratio in expectation
- pipage, randomized pipage: not widely used in practice, mostly theoretical CS -> deploying them in practice is a contribution

5. Experiments / generality / speedups
- real, anonymized data from large classes; much better than course admin's manual solutions across dimensions and metrics
- general beyond education: HR management, diversity of company departments; conflict graph defined by dimension
- experiment: gender diversity in a company's departments
- generality calls for efficient algorithms -> speedup techniques for reasonably large data; work extremely well in practice

6. Discussion
- design decision: conflict graph, maximize conflicts across teams (not friends within teams)
- more modeling flexibility; better models time conflicts among collaborators and diversity constraints

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In big project-based classes, instructors often have to put students into teams and assign the teams to the limited number of projects that they have. Students are happy if they are on a team with friends and they work on a project they like. Also, student teams are efficient if the team members do not have time conflicts, meaning conflicts that come from their class schedule. Usually these assignments are done ad hoc or by hand by some admin, and the admin can spend several days doing it.

Motivated by applications like this in education, we define the problem formally as a combinatorial optimization problem. We assume there are two inputs: the preference graph and the conflict graph. The preference graph captures the preferences of users for projects; it is a bipartite graph and its edge weights are proportional to how much a student likes a project. The conflict graph captures the conflicts between students, so there is a (weighted) edge between two students if they are incompatible. What we want is an assignment of students to projects where every student is assigned to one project and no project gets more students than its capacity. The objective is to maximize the sum of the weights of the preference graph edges that are in the assignment plus the sum of the weights of the conflict edges across the teams that are formed. Students that are assigned to the same project form a team, so we call the problem the Team Formation amidst Conflicts (TFC) problem, and we show that it is NP-hard.

We present an algorithmic framework for approximating TFC. The framework has two steps. In the first step we replace our objective with a concave objective, which can be optimized in polynomial time and gives a fractional solution. In the second step the fractional solution is rounded with dependent-rounding techniques. For the framework to work, the original objective and its concave relaxation have to match on integral inputs.

This kind of general framework is not new. Actually it is inspired by the Max-k-Cut with given part sizes problem. Our problem is in fact the same as Max-k-Cut with given part sizes, except that our objective also has an additional linear term. We show that their approximation algorithm can be applied to our problem. Our contribution is a randomized algorithm that is much more efficient and has a better approximation ratio in expectation.

As far as we know, the dependent-rounding techniques that we use, like pipage and randomized pipage, have not been used much in practical applications; they come mostly from work in theoretical computer science. We think that deploying these techniques in practice is a contribution by itself.

- real, anonymized data from large classes; much better than course admin's manual solutions, across dimensions and metrics

- general beyond education: HR management, more diverse company departments; conflict graph defined by the dimension to diversify
- experiment: gender diversity in a company's departments

- generality -> need efficient algorithms; speedup techniques for reasonably large data; work extremely well in practice

Discussion:
- design decision: conflict graph + maximize conflicts across teams (not friends within teams)
- more modeling flexibility; better models time conflicts among collaborators, diversity constraints

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In big project-based classes, instructors often have to put students into teams and assign the teams to the limited number of projects that they have. Students are happy if they are on a team with friends and they work on a project they like. Also, student teams are efficient if the team members do not have time conflicts, meaning conflicts that come from their class schedule. Usually these assignments are done ad hoc or by hand by some admin, and the admin can spend several days doing it.

Motivated by applications like this in education, we define the problem formally as a combinatorial optimization problem. We assume there are two inputs: the preference graph and the conflict graph. The preference graph captures the preferences of users for projects; it is a bipartite graph and its edge weights are proportional to how much a student likes a project. The conflict graph captures the conflicts between students, so there is a (weighted) edge between two students if they are incompatible. What we want is an assignment of students to projects where every student is assigned to one project and no project gets more students than its capacity. The objective is to maximize the sum of the weights of the preference graph edges that are in the assignment plus the sum of the weights of the conflict edges across the teams that are formed. Students that are assigned to the same project form a team, so we call the problem the Team Formation amidst Conflicts (TFC) problem, and we show that it is NP-hard.

We present an algorithmic framework for approximating TFC. The framework has two steps. In the first step we replace our objective with a concave objective, which can be optimized in polynomial time and gives a fractional solution. In the second step the fractional solution is rounded with dependent-rounding techniques. For the framework to work, the original objective and its concave relaxation have to match on integral inputs.

This kind of general framework is not new. Actually it is inspired by the Max-k-Cut with given part sizes problem. Our problem is in fact the same as Max-k-Cut with given part sizes, except that our objective also has an additional linear term. We show that their approximation algorithm can be applied to our problem. Our contribution is a randomized algorithm that is much more efficient and has a better approximation ratio in expectation.

As far as we know, the dependent-rounding techniques that we use, like pipage and randomized pipage, have not been used much in practical applications; they come mostly from work in theoretical computer science. We think that deploying these techniques in practice is a contribution by itself.

We use real, anonymized data from large classes to show that our algorithms work very well in practice. In the experiments, the solutions we get are much better than the manual solutions made by a course admin, across different dimensions and metrics.

Our problem formulation is general and goes beyond education. For example, we can use the framework in human-resource management to make departments in companies more diverse; we can define the conflict graph depending on the dimension that we want to diversify across. In the experiments we show how to get gender diversity in a company's departments with this idea.

Since the framework is so general, we need efficient algorithms. Part of our contribution is a set of speedup techniques that let us apply our approximation algorithms to reasonably large data. The experimental evaluation shows that these techniques work very well in practice.

Discussion: We note that it was our own design decision to use the conflict graph and maximize conflicts across teams, instead of maximizing friends within teams. We think this choice gives more modeling flexibility to apply the model to many settings. For example, the conflict graph is a better model for time conflicts among collaborators and for diversity constraints.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In large project-based classes, instructors often need to create teams of students and assign them to the finite number of projects they have available. Students are happy if they are in a team with friends and work on a project they like. In addition, student teams are efficient if there are no time conflicts between the team members, i.e., conflicts that stem from their class schedules. Traditionally, such assignments are done in an ad hoc manner or manually by some admin, who can spend several days on the task.

Motivated by such applications in education, we formally define the above problem as a combinatorial optimization problem. We assume two inputs: the preference graph and the conflict graph. The former captures the preferences of users to projects; it is a bipartite graph with edge weights proportional to how much a student likes a project. The latter captures the conflicts between students, i.e., there is a (weighted) edge between two students if they are incompatible. Our goal is to find an assignment of students to projects such that every student is assigned to one project and no project is assigned more students than its capacity. The objective is to maximize the sum of the weights of the preference graph edges that participate in the assignment and the sum of the weights of the conflict edges across the formed teams. Since students assigned to the same project form a team, we call this problem the Team Formation amidst Conflicts (TFC) problem, and we show that it is NP-hard.

In this paper, we present an algorithmic framework for approximating TFC. The framework consists of two steps: first, our objective is replaced by a concave objective, which can be optimized in polynomial time and produces a fractional solution. Then, the fractional solution is rounded using dependent-rounding techniques [1,2]. For our framework to work, we need the original objective and its concave relaxation to match on integral inputs.

This general framework is not new; in fact, it is inspired by the Max-k-Cut with given part sizes problem [1]. Our problem is identical to Max-k-Cut with given part sizes, except that we also have an additional linear term in our objective. We show that their approximation algorithm can be applied to our problem. Our contribution is a much more efficient randomized algorithm with a better approximation ratio in expectation.

To the best of our knowledge, the dependent-rounding techniques we use here, such as pipage and randomized pipage, have not been widely used in practical applications; they primarily stem from work in theoretical computer science [1,3]. We see the deployment of these techniques in practice as a contribution in itself.

Using real, anonymized data from large classes, we demonstrate that our algorithms work extremely well in practice. In our experiments, we show that our solutions are much better than the manual solutions produced by a course admin, across different dimensions and metrics.

Our problem formulation is general and goes beyond educational settings. For example, our framework can be used in human-resource management to increase the diversity of departments in companies; depending on the dimension across which we want to diversify, we can define the conflict graph appropriately. In our experiments, we show how to achieve gender diversity in a company's departments using this idea.

The generality of our framework calls for efficient algorithms. Part of our contribution is a set of speedup techniques that allow us to apply our approximation algorithms to reasonably large data, and in our experimental evaluation we demonstrate that these techniques work extremely well in practice.

Discussion: We note that it was a design decision on our part to consider the conflict graph and maximize conflicts across teams (instead of friends within teams). We believe this choice gives us greater modeling flexibility to apply our model to a variety of settings. For example, the conflict graph better models time conflicts among collaborators as well as diversity constraints.

References:
[1] Ageev and Sviridenko (2004) Alexander A Ageev and Maxim I Sviridenko. 2004. Pipage rounding: A new method of constructing algorithms with proven performance guarantee. Journal of Combinatorial Optimization 8 (2004), 307–328.
[2] Gandhi et al . (2002) Rajiv Gandhi, Samir Khuller, Srinivasan Parthasarathy, and Aravind Srinivasan. 2002. Dependent rounding in bipartite graphs. In The 43rd Annual IEEE Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science, 2002. Proceedings. IEEE, 323–332.
[3] Chekuri et al . (2010) Chandra Chekuri, Jan Vondrák, and Rico Zenklusen. 2010. Dependent randomized rounding via exchange properties of combinatorial structures. In 2010 IEEE 51st Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science . IEEE, 575–584.
